newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Marshall Plan anchored Austrian democracy.
newsitem.headline: Marshall Plan anchored Austrian democracy.

text.p: The U.S. Marshall Plan, honoured at a ceremony in The Hague on Wednesday, helped guarantee Austrian democracy and prosperity with the economy in shreds in 1945 and the threat of communism on its doorstep.

Historians say the Marshall Plan anchored Austria's political freedom at a time when Europe was poised to split into ideological blocs, and laid the foundations for it to become one of Europe's richest and most stable countries.

Austria, absorbed into Adolf Hitler's Third Reich in 1938, received nearly one billion dollars in U.S. aid over four years from 1948 as part of a huge project to rebuild the shattered economies of Western Europe, devised by former U.S. general and secretary of state George Marshall.
In comparison, Britain got $3.2 billion, France $2.7 billion and Germany $1.3 billion in indirect aid, comprising mainly food and raw materials.

"For Austria the Marshall Plan aid meant a decisive step on the way to economic recovery after the destruction of the war and the return to the international community as a democratic state," Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima said in a statement.
Klima was among European and North American leaders attending a ceremony in the Hague to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan.
In fact, Austria may have benefited from the U.S. plan more than any other country in Europe, Guenter Bischof, Associate Professor of History at New Orleans University told Reuters.
"It was one of the poorest countries in the region at the time due to the destruction of the war," said Bischof, who is attending a history conference in Vienna.
The United States and its World War Two allies Britain, France and the Soviet Union occupied Austria from 1945 to 1955.
Many historians regard the Marshall plan as instrumental in checking the spread of communism westwards.

"The Marshall Plan was primarily a political programme to contain communism in Western European countries by stabilising the existing economies or by helping to transform economies and industries destroyed by the war," Vienna University history professor Oliver Ratkolb said.
Austria received $132 per capita, compared with $18 per capita in Germany, which had to repay its Marshall Plan loans, unlike most other recipients.

"Austria was unusual because it received so much per capita, and also because the Soviet zone in eastern Austria participated, which ensured the future unity of the country," Bischof noted. Eastern Germany, under Soviet occupation, was forbidden to take part in the plan.

Industries in Eastern European countries such as former Czechoslovakia, although better off than Austria's at the end of the war, rapidly slid into decline as they were denied access to the U.S. relief plan.
Austria ploughed some 60 percent of the aid into industry, notably the electricity, textile and steel and iron sectors. Much of the rest went into small business and food relief.

"The main point for Austria was that through the Marshall Plan it was able to overcome the wounds of war at least 10 years earlier than it would have otherwise," said Kurt Loeffler, head of Austria's European Recovery Programme (ERP) fund in the Transport and Science ministry.

In 1962, the ERP fund was set up to loan cash to companies at favourable interest rates and it still exists today as an extension of the Marshall Plan. Loeffler said around 80 billion schillings ($6.7 billion) had been pumped into the economy through these revolving funds over the past 35 years. ($ = 11.98 Austrian Schillings)
